# An epic and its stories

Follow this once the owner has accepted lane L for a request. An epic is one large piece of work cut into two to ten stories; no work is started here. It ends with the epic and every story queued as draft tickets in one pull request.

1. Interview the owner about the whole epic, one question at a time as `./ask.md` says: why this work is wanted, for whom, what the owner forbids (the Vetoes), and what the owner has already settled for every story (the Decisions). These four are open questions; ask each only when the request did not already answer it. An answer that settles a choice for every story is a Decision, never a line of Intent: keep it with the owner's own sentence.
2. Read the code once: dispatch `accord-scout` once for the whole epic with the interview's answers, asking for every existing file and folder each part of the epic is expected to change. Check its reply as `./scout.md` step 1 says, with `accord scout check "<file>"` and no `--ticket`, since no id exists yet; on exit 1 follow its step 2. Name in the `## New files` section the files the epic creates.
3. Propose the split: two to ten stories. Each has a title in business language, one to five lines of Intent, the earlier stories it waits for (its `depends_on`), and the files and folders it is likely to touch (its `touches`, a folder ends in `/`), taken from the checked reply and the new files. Stories that touch the same file, or where one story's folder holds the other's file or folder, wait for each other with `after`: the later story lists the earlier one, directly or through another story; the command refuses the split when they do not. When most of the code the epic needs does not exist yet, story 1 is a foundation story that fixes the interfaces (the types, signatures, data shapes and file layout the others use) and every other story waits for it.
4. Write the split file outside the working tree, for example in the system temporary folder, in English, as YAML with the keys `title`, `intent`, `vetoes`, `decisions` and `stories`: `intent`, `vetoes` and `decisions` are lists of lines, and each story has a `title`, an `intent` list, `after`, the numbers of the earlier stories it waits for, and `touches`, a list of paths. Write each Decision as `<decision> — "<the owner's sentence>"`, a faithful English translation of the owner's words when they were not in English, with no `D-` number: the command numbers them D-01, D-02 in order. Leave `decisions` out when the owner settled nothing. When config.yml has `people`, follow `./ids.md` for the creator's initials and give no id; with no `people`, or with ids from a tracker, give an `id` on the epic and on every story: the next free one, or the tracker key the owner names.
5. Once the split file is written, dispatch `accord-critic` once in mode `split`, with the split file and the checked scout reply. It reports stories that edit the same code without a `depends_on`, missed logical dependencies and stories that cannot stand alone. There is no second round: whatever it reports is shown to the owner with the split, and the owner decides.
6. Show the owner the epic title, its Intent lines, its Vetoes, its Decisions and the stories in order, each with the stories it waits for and what it touches, in plain words, with the critic's findings, and ask for approval as `./ask.md` says. Change the split file as the owner asks and show it again, without another critic pass. Never add a point the owner did not make.
7. Only on an explicit yes to the split shown in step 6, run `accord new ticket --type epic --lane L --split <file> --queue` as `./similar.md` says: it prints the similar tickets of the epic and of every story and writes nothing until you judge them; run it again with `--related <id>` or `--related none`. On any other exit 2, show the message and stop: nothing was written or pushed. On exit 0 it has pushed one commit holding the epic, with its Decisions numbered and its `## Approach` listing the stories in order with what each waits for and touches, and every story to one backlog branch, and printed the `branch:`, `base:`, `title:` and `merge:` lines and the ticket paths.
8. Run `accord pr <the epic's id>`, which reads the epic from the backlog branch: on exit 2 show its message and stop. Write each section a `remaining:` line names into the body file it printed, from the epic's Intent and the split, and nothing more. Open the pull request when `gh` is available with `gh pr create --head <branch> --base <base> --title "<title>" --body-file "<body-file>"`, using the `title:` and `body-file:` lines of `accord pr`, not those of step 7; otherwise show the `branch:` line and ask the owner to open it with that title and body. Read the `merge:` line as `/accord queue <idea>` does: `merge: at-once` merges it with `gh pr merge <branch>` and the strategy of `git.merge`; `merge: owner` says the pull request waits for a person.
9. Report the epic id, each story id with the stories it waits for, and the pull request. Say each story is picked up later with `/accord pick-up <id>`, in its own worktree and pull request, in parallel when nothing it waits for is unfinished, and that each story then runs lane M: its own intent interview, approach, plan and review.

## Rules

- The epic itself gets no approach and no plan critique: the one split pass of step 5 is its only critic, the owner's yes to the split is its approval; each story its usual critique when it is picked up, and its scout, planner and reviewers read the epic's Vetoes and Decisions by themselves.
- Run the command only after the explicit yes to the split shown in step 6; a changed split needs a new yes.
- Never claim, start or build a story here, never merge with admin rights, and never push by hand: the command pushes.
